scope: Offline operational and emergency reference for the Burney Falls PCT access to Ash Camp route. It complements live conditions; it never converts a stale report into an all-clear.

operationalRules.title: Follow the checked-in PCTA route, not an old Garmin export
operationalRules.detail: The active plan is the 51.844-mile PCTA-marker itinerary. Garmin files stay comparison evidence only. If a map, app, or person disagrees, stop treating the number as authoritative until it is reconciled.

operationalRules.title: Refresh conditions, then make a human go/no-go call
operationalRules.detail: Water reports, smoke, fires, crossings, campsite availability, road access, and closures have different update paths. A responding feed is not a safety certification.

operationalRules.title: Day 3 is a support operation, not an overnight plan
operationalRules.detail: Travel continuously through the private-timberland corridor with day packs. Do not camp, wait, or treat the Bartle Gap field pin as a casual pickup.

operationalRules.title: Ash Camp is the finish and vehicle extraction point
operationalRules.detail: Finish at the PCTA route boundary, then use the separately verified Ash Camp / FS 38N11 field pickup plan. Do not assume the road is suitable for the Kia Sportage until it is checked 24–48 hours beforehand.

dayFocus.title: Start deliberately after the long approach drive
dayFocus.detail: The opening mileage is short on purpose. Verify the Burney entry, PCT connector, Lake Britton/Pit No. 3 crossing, and the current water report before moving.

dayFocus.title: Protect the largest climbing day and carry through camp
dayFocus.detail: This is the biggest ascent. The pre-private site is GIS-screened rather than ground-approved; inspect durable surface, hazards, capacity, and water before committing.

dayFocus.title: Execute the supported private-corridor traverse
dayFocus.detail: Carry day packs only, move continuously, meet the driver at the exact field pin, sleep legally off-corridor, and return to the same crossing before Day 4. Dense brush and blowdown remain an explicit field check.

dayFocus.title: Re-enter exactly where Day 3 exited
dayFocus.detail: Return to the same Bartle Gap crossing before climbing to the high saddle. Treat the dry camp and water plan as current-condition decisions, not reserved sites.

dayFocus.title: Control the descent even though mileage is short
dayFocus.detail: The day is mostly downhill. Use poles, short steps, and a deliberate pace; do not let the lower mileage disguise knee load.

dayFocus.title: Budget for mixed vertical on accumulated fatigue
dayFocus.detail: This is a mixed up-and-down day, not a flat recovery. Refresh water evidence and evaluate the group before leaving camp.

dayFocus.title: Treat this as the knee-protection day
dayFocus.detail: The route loses roughly 343 feet per mile. Slow the descent, maintain spacing, and make pole use a group default rather than an afterthought.

dayFocus.title: Finish to the actual Ash Camp pickup
dayFocus.detail: The final morning still descends substantially. Hit the canonical finish, then use a driver who has already confirmed FS 38N11, gates, turnaround, weather, and vehicle suitability.

emergency.disclaimer: This is a coordination reference, not medical treatment instruction. In an emergency, use the fastest available emergency channel.

actions.title: Immediate threat to life or property
actions.detail: Call 911 when cellular service is available. Without service, activate the tested satellite SOS device and keep the group together unless staying creates a greater immediate danger.

actions.title: Send the facts that rescuers need
actions.detail: Send the exact coordinate, PCT and route mile, condition, injuries or hazards, party count, intended movement, and battery / communication status. Do not replace facts with a vague 'help' message.

actions.title: Preserve navigation and communication capability
actions.detail: Keep one phone and the satellite device powered, protect them from water and cold, and write down the last confirmed location if screens or batteries fail.

actions.title: Notify the preassigned contact only after emergency contact is underway
actions.detail: Use the actual team contact tree and check-in protocol after the emergency channel is engaged. The app deliberately does not invent a family contact or a rescue ETA.

contacts.title: Emergency services
contacts.when: Life-threatening emergency when cellular service is available.

contacts.title: Shasta County Sheriff's dispatch
contacts.when: Non-emergency support or coordination; do not use instead of 911 for an emergency.

contacts.title: Poison Control
contacts.when: Possible poisoning or exposure; use 911 for collapse, seizure, trouble breathing, or inability to awaken.

contacts.title: McArthur-Burney Falls Memorial State Park
contacts.when: Start-side access, reservations, and park notices; not a substitute for emergency dispatch.

contacts.title: McCloud Ranger Station
contacts.when: FS 38N11 / Ash Camp road suitability and forest access questions before pickup.

checkInProtocol.title: Before departure: test it, do not assume it
checkInProtocol.detail: Send one real satellite outbound message and receive an acknowledgement. Put each hiker's phone, offline map, charging cable, and emergency contact list through the same test.

checkInProtocol.title: Each hiking day: use a named cadence
checkInProtocol.detail: Agree on a start, destination, and end-of-day check-in before leaving camp. Record missed check-ins and any route/condition change in Field → Ops Log when signal returns.

checkInProtocol.title: Day 3: driver and hikers share the same no-contact rule
checkInProtocol.detail: The driver receives the field pin, target window, re-entry time, and no-show rule before the hikers enter the private corridor. No one waits or camps on private land.

checkInProtocol.title: Ash Camp: confirm driver movement before the final descent
checkInProtocol.detail: Confirm road suitability and pickup timing before Day 8. Send the finishing message from the PCTA boundary; do not promise an exact arrival time based on an unverified road.

offlineLimitations: This bundle retains the confirmed itinerary and official sources but cannot see a same-day closure, road gate, fire order, smoke plume, water flow, campsite occupancy, passenger check-in, baggage, or live airline gate change unless Flight Watch is refreshed.
A live condition snapshot has an explicit fetched time and source status. If it is stale, missing, or marked manual-required, perform that named check before treating it as usable.
Keep a separate offline topographic/navigation map on every hiker's phone; this app is an operational companion, not the only navigation tool.

dayThreeSupport.instruction: DECISION 2026-08-05: Day 3 is now an unsupported power-through. No driver, no pack transfer, no off-corridor lodging, no exact-pin pickup, no next-morning re-entry. The team walks the private corridor continuously with full packs and camps on public land at Moosehead Creek. This reverses the earlier supported-traverse plan, which was itself adopted to replace an unsupported leg — the decision is back where it started, but now with measured numbers rather than assumptions. What made it defensible: the driver only ever bought 1.34 miles and the ability to carry day packs, because Sierra Pacific ground ENDS at PCT 1447.738, just 0.207 mile (about 365 yards) past the old Bartle Gap pin. Legal ground was always a five-minute walk beyond the pickup point.
dayThreeSupport.estimatedHours: 9.25–11 hours with full packs at 1.85 mph over effort-adjusted distance
dayThreeSupport.finishCamp: Moosehead Creek, PCT 1448.873, USFS public land
dayThreeSupport.cost: This is now the hardest day of the trip by a wide margin: 13.933 miles and 9.25–11 hours carrying full overnight packs, against 6–7.25 hours on the next hardest day. Start at first light. There is no bailout in the middle because there is nowhere legal to stop.
dayThreeSupport.waterRule: Fully self-supported. There is no legal collection anywhere between Peavine (1434.236) and Moosehead (1448.873) — Clark, Deadman, and Kosk all sit on private timberland. That is a 14.6-mile carry that must also cover the Day 2 dry camp, dinner, and breakfast: roughly 10–11 L per person at peak load leaving Peavine. Two extra collapsible reservoirs are not optional under this plan.
requiredBeforeStart: Every hiker carries the full Peavine-to-Moosehead water load; nobody is bringing more.
All three agree to a first-light start, because 11 hours from a 7:00 AM start finishes at 6:00 PM.
Moosehead Creek is ground-verified for a legal, durable three-person site and confirmed flowing in the final-week water pull.
Everyone knows the Peavine off-trail water offset at 41.06012, -121.78501 before Day 2.
dayThreeSupport.bailoutRule: There is no legal stopping point inside the corridor, so the plan is simply to keep walking. If someone cannot continue, the nearest legal ground is USFS land beginning at PCT 1447.738 — reachable from anywhere in the second half of the day — and the pre-screened emergency site sits near route mile 27.791 at 41.177527, -121.827003. Escalate by satellite before improvising.
dayThreeSupport.groupPaceReality: THE ESTIMATE ASSUMES A PACE THIS GROUP MAY NOT HOLD. The 9.25-11 hour figure comes from 1.85 mph over 15.09 effort-adjusted miles, which is a reasonable loaded pace for a fit adult carrying a normal pack. On Day 3 nobody is carrying a normal pack: peak load leaving Peavine is roughly 57 lb per person (about 20 lb base, 15 lb food, 22 lb water). The group also spans ages 34, 36, and 75, and a group moves at its slowest member. Recompute honestly: at 1.7 mph Day 3 runs 10-12 h and a 6:00 AM start finishes 4:00-6:00 PM. At 1.6 mph it is 10.5-12.75 h, finishing 4:30-6:45 PM. At 1.5 mph it is 11.25-13.5 h, finishing 5:15-7:30 PM against a 7:33 PM sunset — no margin at all. At 1.4 mph the day ends after dark. A 57 lb pack plausibly puts a 75-year-old at or below 1.5 mph, and that is load physics rather than a comment about fitness. Consequences: start at first light, not 6:00 AM; every hiker carries a working headlamp within reach rather than buried; and shifting water off the heaviest-loaded hiker protects the group pace more than any other single decision. If a shakedown hike before the trip shows the group at 1.5 mph or slower under load, the honest reading is that unsupported Day 3 has no daylight margin and the supported plan deserves a second look.
dayThreeSupport.recommendedStart: First light, about 6:15-6:30 AM civil twilight on Aug 31, rather than a nominal 6:00 AM clock start

finishPlan.pickupWindow: about 9:30 AM–12:30 PM after a 6:30–7:00 AM start
finishPlan.road: FS Road 38N11 / Hawkins Creek Road is unpaved and can be rough. Do not commit the Kia Sportage unless the McCloud Ranger Station confirms current suitability 24–48 hours before pickup.

driveSnapshot.source: OSRM road-routing snapshot carried in the generated runtime bundle; live navigation controls on travel day.

finishPlan.fallback: A local high-clearance driver or taxi is a secondary plan only after that provider explicitly accepts the Ash Camp / FS 38N11 assignment. Trail angels are a named-and-confirmed tertiary backup, not transportation to assume.

gates.title: CONFIRMED — United itinerary verified against the booking
gates.detail: VERIFIED 2026-08-05 against the team's own United record: DAN SJC UA481 - UA1317, scheduled Aug 28 2026 6:03 PM PDT through Sep 7 2026 10:45 AM PDT. That matches the times carried in this file exactly, so no correction is needed anywhere. Nothing further is required before travel day beyond the ordinary live check: use United Flight Status on Aug 28 for delay, gate, and terminal changes, since a material delay still shifts Mikaela's airport pickup and how much sleep the team gets before the 5:00 AM departure.
gates.blocks: Nothing. The itinerary is booked and verified.

gates.title: Aug 28 rest stop CONFIRMED at Gunnar's place in Campbell — still decide Mikaela's return leg
gates.detail: RESOLVED 2026-08-04: the team sleeps at Gunnar's home in Campbell on Aug 28. No booking is required and no hotel fallback is needed. UA481 reaches SJC at 10:36 PM PDT, Campbell is about 15 minutes from the airport, and the group drives north at about 5:00–5:30 AM Aug 29 rather than driving through the night. Load the vehicle on Aug 28 before the airport run so the 5:00 AM departure is real: every 30 minutes lost here pushes the Day 1 start later into a hot Saturday afternoon and eats the daylight margin at Rock Creek. WHAT REMAINS OPEN is only Mikaela's return leg. About 6.1 hours north, the drop-off, then a 6.1-hour return is roughly 12–13 hours of driving for a single driver, on the back of a near-midnight airport pickup. Decide before Aug 21 whether she rests near Burney or Redding before turning around or commits to the same-day return, and treat that as a safety decision with the same weight as the hikers' plan.
gates.blocks: A rested Day 1 start with daylight margin, and a safe return leg for the only driver.

gates.title: Secure Saturday Burney Falls entry and exact PCT connector
gates.detail: August 29 is a Saturday. California State Parks' 2026 pilot requires an advance day-use reservation on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays through September 27; confirm the start-side drop-off and posted trail access too.
gates.blocks: Legal vehicle entry and the actual Day 1 start.

gates.title: Recheck the Lake Britton / Pit No. 3 Dam crossing
gates.detail: CORRECTED 2026-08-04: the bridge-work notice that drove this gate was a 2022 item, not a live one. It read 'Bridge Over Lake Britton Dam to Close April 18–Sept. 2 While PG&E Contractor Improves Bridge Deck' and was dated 05/16/22 — the closure window was April–September 2022, four years ago. The 2026-08-02 water report snapshot no longer carries it at all; the only current entry for mile 1422.4 is 2026-07-09 (Lana) describing poor water access: the lake level is too low to collect from the eastern shore, there is a steep trail to water on the western shore, and the water is dirty with pollen, so fill at the park spigots instead. So the alarming part of this gate was stale and is now retired. The gate itself stays OPEN for a narrower and real reason: PG&E performs recurring maintenance on this dam crossing, the water report is not an authority on bridge status, and a 2022 closure in the same calendar window is evidence that such work recurs in exactly this season. Confirm the crossing is open and unescorted with PG&E, the park, and current PCTA closures in the final week — do not treat the absence of a notice in a water report as confirmation that it is open.
gates.blocks: The intended Day 1 route if the crossing is closed or escorted. No longer blocked by the retired 2022 notice.

gates.title: RESOLVED — Day 3 support retired in favour of powering through
gates.detail: CLOSED 2026-08-05 by decision, not by booking. No driver is needed and none will be arranged. Day 3 becomes a 13.933-mile unsupported traverse with full packs, finishing on public land at Moosehead Creek. The reasoning: the assessor screen showed Sierra Pacific ground ends at PCT 1447.738, only 0.207 mile past the Bartle Gap pin, so the entire support operation was buying 1.34 miles and day packs — not, as the plan had implied, the only legal way to finish the day. The cost of this choice is real and is recorded in dayThreeSupport: Day 3 is now the hardest day of the trip at 9.25–11 hours under load, and the water carry becomes fully self-supported at roughly 10–11 L per person. What it removes is an entire dependency chain — a named driver, a booked off-corridor overnight, road and gate verification, an exact field pin, a timed pickup window, a no-contact protocol, and a next-morning re-entry — every link of which could have failed on the day.
gates.blocks: Nothing. This gate no longer blocks the route.

gates.title: Rebuild the Day 2–3 water carry around a dry Clark Spring, and revalidate every overnight camp
gates.detail: The 2026-08-02 PCT Water Report changes this materially. CLARK SPRING (PCT 1438.462) IS REPORTED DRY as of 2026-07-10 — it still had 'nice flow, deep pool' on 2026-06-21, so it dries mid-summer and will very likely still be dry on Aug 31. Do not plan a top-up there. But flow is the smaller half of this problem, because EVERY REMAINING SOURCE ON DAY 3 SITS ON PRIVATE TIMBERLAND. The Shasta County assessor screen places Clark Spring (1438.43) and Deadman Creek (1440.47) on Hearst Forests, and Kosk Spring (1442.01) on Pondosa Forest LLC; Kosk also requires a 2/10-mile off-trail walk to reach. The active PCTA alert allows passage on these lands but prohibits camping, fires, stoves, smoking, and extended stops, and requires continuous travel — so none of the three is a plannable collection point, and a mapped spring icon is not permission. The continuously private corridor runs from about trip mile 14.923 to 26.953 (roughly PCT 1435.6 to 1447.6), about 12.03 miles, and the first public water after it is Moosehead Creek (1448.873, USFS). The real planning span is therefore Peavine (1434.236) to the driver's staged water at Bartle Gap (1447.531): about 13.3 trail miles with no legal collection stop, and that span must also cover a dry overnight, dinner, and breakfast for three. If the Day 3 driver fails to appear, the span becomes Peavine to Moosehead at about 14.6 miles. The driver must therefore carry a full reserve for all three hikers even if every middle source is usable, because usable and legal are different questions here. A separate weak point sits on Day 5: Alder Creek / Star City Creek (1456.312) is the water the Day 5 camp is named for, and its only 2026 sighting is 2026-06-15 ('a clear pool of water and flowing clear water, 2 liters per minute') — the oldest evidence behind any planned source, roughly eleven weeks before the team arrives on Sep 2. Verify it in the final-week pull and carry a contingency from Deer Creek if it cannot be confirmed. Clark was the last intermediate on the public-land side of that question and it is now gone. SEPARATELY, PEAVINE IS A WALK-PAST HAZARD: it is 'absolutely dry where trail crosses the creek' (Lana, 2026-07-10) and the flowing water sits off-trail at 41.06012, -121.78501 — 'in the bushes to the right just off second road crossing' (Mobber, 2026-07-15). Two independent 2026 reports agree. Brief all three hikers on that offset before Day 2 or someone will cross a dry bed and keep walking. Every observation above is from JULY 2026 and the trip is Aug 29–Sep 5, six to seven weeks deeper into the dry season, so treat marginal sources as worse, never better. Re-pull pctwater.com and FarOut in the final week. The pre-private site remains GIS-screened, not ground-approved, and the water plan must still work without assuming any collection inside the private corridor.
gates.blocks: A survivable Day 2 dry camp and the Day 3 water reserve. This gate is no longer just verification: the carry itself needs rebuilding.

gates.title: Verify FS Road 38N11 and Ash Camp pickup vehicle suitability
gates.detail: Ash Camp is the defined finish, not an arbitrary 52nd-mile exit. Confirm road condition, gate status, turnaround, weather, daylight, and Kia Sportage suitability with McCloud Ranger Station before driving in.

gates.title: Test satellite communicator, contact tree, and no-contact protocol
gates.detail: Send an actual outbound and acknowledgement test, keep the shared itinerary and emergency contacts offline, and make sure every hiker knows the Day 3 and Ash Camp message cadence.
gates.blocks: Reliable coordination when cell service is unavailable.

gates.due: Before Aug 21, then recheck the week of departure
gates.title: Get a California Campfire Permit each — fire restrictions are already active
gates.detail: ANSWERED AND ACTIONABLE. Shasta-Trinity Forest Order 14-26-07 took effect July 1, 2026 and covers the whole forest, including this route. It prohibits building, maintaining, or attending any fire, campfire, or stove fire; the listed exceptions (Shasta/Trinity/Iron Canyon lakeshores and the Yolla Bolla-Middle Eel, Chanchelulla, Castle Crags, and Trinity Alps Wilderness areas) do not cover the Burney Falls to Ash Camp corridor. A portable gas, propane, or pressurized-fuel stove with a shut-off valve is still legal, but ONLY for a hiker holding a valid California Campfire Permit, and only with at least five feet of clearance from anything flammable. The permit is free and issued online. All three hikers need one, carried, not left at home. Campfires are simply out. Smoking is prohibited except inside a vehicle or while stopped in a cleared area at least three feet across, which is stricter than most people assume and matches the private-timberland rule anyway. Restrictions tighten as September approaches rather than easing, so recheck the order in the departure week and carry a cold-soak option so a further tightening never becomes a food problem.
gates.blocks: Any hot food on the route. Without a permit each, the stove is dead weight and using it is a violation.
